extracted.intended_audience: geophysicists, physical geographers, geologists, and scientific readers of Nature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and presentation of a theoretical geophysical model using spherical harmonic analysis to account for the distribution of continental and oceanic regions and related geological implications. Focuses on assumptions, method of discretization and harmonic decomposition, comparison with observed features, and interpretation of dynamical causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement and justification of model assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is solved 'on the suppositions that the density is uniform and the initial stress is hydrostatic pressure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper should state its simplifying assumptions clearly (e.g., uniform density, hydrostatic initial stress) and discuss their applicability and limitations for a planetary body of Earth's size. Reviewers should check whether these assumptions are appropriate for the claims made and whether the consequences of relaxing them are acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical criterion for gravitational instability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the resistance to compression is sufficiently small the body is unstable, leading to concentration of mass or hemispheric density differences; for an Earth-sized body the material must be as compressible as granite for such instability to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the paper quantifies the required resistance to compression and compares that to known material properties (e.g., granite compressibility and measured pressures). Check numerical plausibility of claims about when gravitational instability would occur and whether empirical constraints (earthquake propagation, geodesy) are used appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spherical harmonics as standard deformation patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Spherical harmonics specify standard patterns of deformation: first degree (hemispheric shift), second degree (ellipsoid), third degree (four standard types: zonal, tesseral rank 1, tesseral rank 2, sectorial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether spherical harmonics are presented and applied correctly as basis functions (degrees mapped to interpretable deformation patterns). Verify the mapping between harmonic degrees/types and geographic features claimed (e.g., zonal harmonic associated with Antarctic continent and Arctic Ocean).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data discretization and coding method for harmonic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface was divided into 2502 small areas; areas above sea were given +1, those below the 1400-fathom line given -1, and intermediate areas 0, and the distribution was analysed for harmonics of degrees 1–3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the choice of discretization (number and size of areas), threshold(s) (e.g., 1400-fathom line), and coding (+1/0/-1). Evaluate sensitivity of results to those choices and whether the method's 'roughness' or potential biases are acknowledged and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction and comparison of theoretical vs. empirical patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite theoretical curve of separation between continental and oceanic regions (from harmonics) should resemble the smoothed empirical curve representing the parts to be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess similarity between model-predicted curves/maps and observed/smoothed empirical representations; check both qualitative resemblance and quantitative differences (regions where computed elevation is too small or too large). Consider whether deviations are explained by model limitations or missing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of harmonic amplitudes and geographic associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis informs on positions and relative magnitudes (e.g., central region of greatest elevation ~Crimea; equatorial depression and two great basins; third-degree harmonics produce furrows/ridges associated with continents/oceans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the paper convincingly links particular harmonics and their amplitudes to observable geographic features (Pacific, Atlantic, Antarctica, etc.), and whether such associations are supported by the analysis rather than post hoc interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of expected relative magnitudes of harmonics
rubrics_metrics.description: One would expect inequalities expressed by harmonics of the third degree to be much smaller than those of the first and second degrees, but the analysis shows all three inequalities are comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review whether the work articulates dynamical expectations for harmonic magnitudes and examines discrepancies between expectation and computed results. Check whether inferred secular changes or historical processes are a plausible explanation for unexpected relative magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and discussion of limitations and alternative causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreement of theory with facts is not perfect; reasons include the roughness of the harmonic analysis method and the fact that many other causes must have contributed to shaping continents and oceans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the manuscript candidly acknowledges methodological limitations and alternative geological causes. A good paper should discuss sources of error, the impact of neglected effects, and where additional data or refined methods might change conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive geological and geomorphological implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should offer explanations for features such as the difference between Atlantic and Pacific coast types, alternations of sea and land in geological history, and possible secular changes (e.g., subsidences near Crimea, changing ocean extents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the model yields testable geological predictions and whether those predictions are consistent with independent geological evidence (coast types, coral reef behavior, inferred subsidence). Prefer models that connect dynamical causes to observable phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of mechanisms for secular change
rubrics_metrics.description: Secular changes in the inequalities (first/second vs. third degree) are argued to be brought about by seismic and volcanic activities (relief of strain) and by the diminishing speed of Earth's rotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether proposed mechanisms for long-term change (seismic/volcanic activity, viscous relaxation, rotational slowing) are physically plausible and quantitatively sufficient to produce the inferred transformations. Check consistency with geodesy and geological time scales.
